title: What Suno’s Studio update changes for hands-on creators
question: How might October’s Studio changes affect musicians who bring their own ideas into Suno?
argument: Suno announced more precise clip timing, stretching, and fades on October 8. Those controls address editing tasks that matter to creators working from their own recordings or generated material. Earlier practitioner accounts show why such control could be useful, but they do not test the new features.
synthesis: Suno’s release note describes timeline controls, while Todd Edwards describes cutting up generated material, Zemi describes bringing in his own vocals, and a podcast host describes starting with a guitar recording. Together, these suggest that editing and arranging controls may matter more to these workflows than one-prompt generation. The accounts cannot show whether October’s changes improve their results: none documents a test of those changes.
limitations: The feature descriptions come from Suno’s product marketing. The practitioner accounts describe individual methods and self-reported contributions, without comparable before-and-after tests. The brief lacks an independent test of the October update and the perspective of a creator who tried these controls on a release-bound track.

claims.statement: Suno announced improved downbeat detection for new clips, shift-drag clip stretching, and adjustable fade curves in Studio.

locator.quote: Better down-beat detection
shift-click-dragging automatically timestretches a clip
Now, you can shape the curve by dragging the node on the fade icon

claims.statement: In a MusicRadar interview published before the October update, producer Todd Edwards said he puts musical ideas into Suno, then cuts up the output as samples. His account describes his method, not a test of the new controls.

locator.quote: But I can put ideas in, make my own disco or soft rock songs, then take that out, cut them up and use them as samples

claims.statement: Zemi told Dazed that he sings and produces material, uses Suno to change his voice, and mixes the result himself. This is his account of his contribution, not an independently verified breakdown.

locator.quote: I sing the songs, bring it over into Suno to change the voice, and then mix it myself.

claims.statement: In an October 5 podcast demonstration, Caleb Porzio described recording a short guitar idea before using Suno.

The October editing controls could help creators shape material that begins with their own performances or ideas: Suno describes controls for aligning and reshaping clips, while separate practitioners describe recording, transforming, or sampling material. These sources establish a plausible workflow fit, not an observed improvement from the update.

locator.quote: This is useful for matching samples and found sounds with tracks in Studio projects, regardless of the tempo.
But I can put ideas in, make my own disco or soft rock songs, then take that out, cut them up and use them as samples

title: What Suno quality tests can actually tell a songwriter
question: Do recent Suno tests show better sound or more control for a creator working from their own song?
argument: The tests measure different things. WaveDisco compares loudness and peaks across model versions and export formats. Ytyng measures spectral balance across tracks made with different prompts and codecs. Two video creators test whether Suno follows their musical direction. Together, these accounts reveal specific behavior to check in a creator's own work, but they do not support an overall v6 quality score.
synthesis: WaveDisco's flat LUFS and True Peak results across its model comparison do not settle whether a song sounds good; ytyng explicitly separates its spectral measurements from that judgment. The video demonstrations add a different question: whether an output follows a particular melody or performance instruction. The cross-source inference is that release readiness needs separate checks for export levels, audible artifacts, and adherence to the creator's intent. These small, differently controlled tests cannot establish how often Suno will pass those checks across songs or genres.
limitations: WaveDisco measured three songs and had WAV–MP3 comparisons for only two. Ytyng compared v6 exports with older tracks made from different prompts and codecs. The video creators report their own listening judgments without blinded assessment; Andrea Olsen also promotes a music business course in her video. Caleb Porzio's podcast account offers a listener's reaction, not a controlled test. A blinded listening study using matched prompts and exports, including creators across more genres, is still missing.

claims.statement: WaveDisco's author says they regenerated three songs with the same lyrics and prompt across four model versions, then measured LUFS and True Peak; they found no consistent direction in those measures that established v6 as better.

locator.quote: Three songs, four model versions each, same lyrics and prompt every time. I measured LUFS and True Peak on every output with the same audio analysis pipeline, and compared WAV and MP3 formats where I had both.
I came in looking for a clear answer on whether v6 was measurably better than v5.5. On LUFS and True Peak, I didn't find one — the numbers move, but there's no consistent direction I can point to.

claims.statement: In WaveDisco's two songs with format comparisons, the author reports a WAV–MP3 loudness gap on v5.5 that was absent across the tested v6 models, while warning that the result is an illustration rather than a study.

locator.quote: That's six loudness comparisons on the v6 side — three models, two songs — and every one shows the same thing: WAV and MP3 land at the same LUFS. The gap that existed consistently in v5.5 is gone.
To be clear: this is two songs where I had format comparisons. It's an illustration, not a study. Your tracks may behave differently.

claims.statement: Ytyng reports lower high-frequency energy in its v6 export sample, but its older comparison tracks used different prompts and a different codec; the author says the difference could partly or wholly reflect the songs chosen.

locator.quote: v6 was down 2 to 3.4dB at 2 to 12kHz, and the spectral centroid was 36% lower. On the other hand, the reputation of "over-compression" was not supported. What got narrower is the bandwidth, not the dynamics.

The biggest one is that the songs and genres are not controlled. The v6 side is 2 songs and the pre-v6 side is 6 songs, each made from a different prompt. Spectral centroid moves a lot with genre, so I have not ruled out the possibility that part of this difference, or all of it, is "because the songs are different".
As written above, the v6 side is m4a (Opus 132kbps) and the pre-v6 side is mp3 (about 180kbps VBR), and I compare them as they are.

claims.statement: In one Suno song demonstration, the creator added vocal, instrument, and performance directions in stages and judged the later vocal smoother, while acknowledging that another generation of the song might explain the difference.

Producer Andrea Olsen reports that Suno kept her uploaded voice memo's melody and largely followed her worship-song directions, yet she still heard the result as sounding like AI. This is her judgment of one song.

Podcast host Caleb Porzio says he wanted to replay songs made from his rough recordings, but also describes audible artifacts in AI covers he encountered. His account shows why enjoyment and artifact checks can produce different judgments.

Taken together, these accounts support checking export levels, whether the melody and directions survived, and whether audible artifacts remain in each candidate track. They cannot predict how often a different creator's tracks will be release ready, because their samples, settings, formats, and outcomes differ.

locator.quote: Measurements in this article were taken on three specific tracks using the same audio analysis pipeline on the same day. Suno's output characteristics vary across generations even with identical prompts — these numbers reflect one set of outputs, not a guaranteed behavior of any model version.
"How good a song is" has little to do with the spectrum, but this was about the only objective difference I could think of that a machine can measure, so I did it.

title: Before You Upload, Know What You Are Contributing
question: What should an independent creator verify before uploading a song idea or releasing Suno-assisted work, and what evidence should they watch next?
argument: Keep a record of the lyrics, melody, demo, performances, and generated parts you used; review the applicable Suno terms before uploading; and check the receiving platform’s current rules before release. These are separate decisions. A creator’s account of their contributions does not settle contractual rights, copyright status, or how a service will classify the finished track.
synthesis: JG Beats Lab’s Josh proposes a file-by-file record of human and generated contributions. Music Business Worldwide reports Suno’s statement that user creations contributed to v6 training, while Italy’s competition authority has opened an investigation into Suno’s terms. Together, these sources support checking both what enters the service and the terms governing that use. They do not establish that every upload trained v6 or that the authority has found a violation. Deezer’s planned search filter adds a later distribution question, but the supplied report does not show that the filter is live or how it would treat a particular Suno-assisted song.
limitations: The applicable primary Suno terms and a distributor’s current rules are not supplied, so this brief cannot verify contractual rights or give an individual release clearance. The record lacks an independent creator’s documented experience of a Suno-assisted release being classified by Deezer. The podcast host’s workflow is practical advice from a practitioner who also promotes his services, not a legal determination.

claims.statement: JG Beats Lab’s Josh advises creators to keep the original demo, lyric sheet, generation settings, retained stems, raw vocal takes, and final master together, and to identify which parts they wrote or Suno generated.

Suno told media that v6 training included licensed partner content and community interactions including creations and preference signals. This is Suno’s account of its training, not evidence that a particular creator’s upload was used.

locator.quote: v6 was trained on content licensed from our partners, interactions including creations and preference signals from our community, and the accumulated learnings from our team.

claims.statement: On October 6, 2026, the Italian Competition Authority announced an investigation into whether Suno’s terms may be unfair; opening proceedings is not an adverse finding.

locator.quote: The Italian Competition Authority has launched an investigation into Suno Inc., a US company that provides generative AI services specialising in music creation. The proceedings focus on Suno’s Terms of Service. According to the Authority, the terms under investigation may be unfair pursuant to Article 33 of the Consumer Code since they may create a significant imbalance in the rights and obligations under the contract, to the detriment of consumers.

claims.statement: The Los Angeles Times reported that artists’ payouts and the extent of their choice under label AI deals remain undisclosed, while Sony and Universal’s newer infringement claims against Suno remain allegations in litigation. A creator should distinguish a partner’s promised benefit from an observed payout or court ruling.

locator.quote: But so far, none of them have disclosed what artists will be paid, how many artists have opted in, or how much input individual musicians have over whether their work is used.
Sony and Universal also filed a new lawsuit last week alleging that Suno’s latest model still infringes on their copyrighted works.

claims.statement: Inference: documenting human contributions and checking upload terms address different release questions. Josh’s recordkeeping method shows what a creator says they made; Suno’s training account and the Italian investigation show why the service’s treatment of submitted material needs a separate check. These sources cannot establish the rights in any individual finished recording.

locator.quote: Suno said v6 was trained on “interactions including creations and preference signals” from its community.
The contractual provisions on copyright deserve particular attention.

claims.statement: Deezer says it plans to roll out a search toggle for fully AI-generated music before the end of 2026. A creator considering Deezer should watch its eventual classification and release rules; the report does not establish that the toggle is live or that every AI-assisted song falls within it.

locator.quote: Deezer says it is introducing an on/off toggle that will let users exclude fully AI-generated music from their search results.
The French streaming service said on Tuesday (October 13) that the feature will roll out globally before the end of 2026.
Both are open about their use of Suno to modify their vocals, but, crucially, they insist that it’s not that deep – it’s just like reverb or auto-tune.
